findings.where: First screen, the whole hero ground (desktop and phone): the pale blue-to-lavender wash behind the heading, the paragraphs, the margin notes and the photograph
findings.fault: The first screen is the only part of the page not on warm paper. It sits on a cool wash that fades from blue to lilac. Every other section uses the flat ivory, and the tile's own palette card says 'Three colours, no accent' and 'the paper is a flat warm tone'. A lilac gradient reads like a tech start-up or a generic AI template, not a well-set legal brief. It also turns the grey-graded photograph a dull, cold grey on lilac. The tile's spirit (a page set like a legal journal) shows only below the fold, and the founder judges the first screen first.
findings.who_objects: The founder, who asked for a warm paper ground and the house blue and grey as the only ink, and who rejects anything that reads as 'in-your-face techy' or a look any consultancy could own. Mark, whose bank and government readers expect the gravitas of a legal journal, not a SaaS landing page.

findings.where: First screen, Mark's first-person paragraph 'I ADVISE MULTILATERAL DEVELOPMENT BANKS… MELBOURNE LAW SCHOOL.' (four lines of tracked capitals on desktop, eight on phone)
findings.fault: The one paragraph that says who Mark is and whom he serves is set as a long block of spaced-out capitals. When you squint, it is the second-loudest thing on the screen. It shouts like a banner or a firm's tagline rather than reading as a person talking. It also outweighs the calmer serif paragraph under it and the action. A paragraph in all capitals is slow to read, so the key 'what I do, for whom' line is the hardest text on the screen to take in.
findings.who_objects: The founder, whose first test is that Mark is heard in his own voice, not as a corporate label. The development-bank officer doing the 5-second scan, who has to work through capitals to find out what Mark does.

findings.where: Header lockup, top left (desktop and phone): the large aqueduct mark with 'MMM INFRA' placed before 'Mark M. Moseley'
findings.fault: The logo leads and the name follows. The arches come first in reading order and carry more visual weight than 'Mark M. Moseley', which is set small at about nav size beside them. So the first thing a visitor registers is the firm's mark, not the person. This turns round the founder's rule that his name leads with the logo beside it.
findings.who_objects: The founder, who made 'his name leads, with the logo beside it' part of the personal-advisor test that comes before craft. Mark, who wants the individual, not the firm, to be the brand (brand sheet §5).

findings.where: Phone, first screen and hero order: the heading, then the 'Istanbul, 2025' note, the photograph, the capitals paragraph, the 'Melbourne, 2026' note, the risk paragraph, the 'São Paulo, 2024' note, and only then 'Write to me'
findings.fault: On a phone the margin notes become inline lines between the paragraphs. The first phone screen shows the heading, a talk title and the photo, but nothing that says what Mark does or how to reach him. 'Write to me' sits about one and a half screens down. Each note sits as close to the paragraph below it as to the one above, so the notes read as stray captions. The São Paulo note also sits between the last paragraph and the action, which breaks the link between Mark's words and the invitation to write.
findings.who_objects: A bank officer opening Mark's link from LinkedIn on a phone, who cannot tell from the first screen what he advises on, has to scroll past three interruptions to find the one action, and may not scroll that far.

findings.where: Motion specimen (desktop): the curve diagram on the left, and the demo photograph, 'Replay the entrance' and the timing table on the right
findings.fault: The section splits into two columns that do not line up. The demo photograph floats far right and starts lower than the heading. Under the curve on the left, a tall empty block opens while the table runs on in the right column. The curve and the photo it animates look like two unrelated pieces, not one explained move.
findings.who_objects: The founder reviewing the motion sketch, who has to piece the curve, the demo and the table together across a gap to see the one entrance being described.

findings.where: First screen, trust: the paragraph 'I advise multilateral development banks, development agencies and governments…' and the margin notes
findings.fault: The first screen shows no third-party proof and names no body Mark has worked for. It gives only the generic classes 'multilateral development banks, development agencies and governments' and three talk titles. Nothing shows who asked for his work, so the claim of advising banks rests on his word alone.
findings.who_objects: Procurement-minded staff at a development bank, who judge an advisor by who asked him and where. They see a category claim on the first screen rather than a checkable specific.
